item.title: Chinese FM rejects Philippine claims about disruptions of medical evacuation near Ren'ai Jiao, vows to safeguard sovereignty and maritime rights
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-09 16:25:00
Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning A Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson on Friday rejected Philippine claims about disruptions of a medical evacuation from a Philippine vessel illegally grounded at China's Ren'ai Jiao, stressing China will firmly respond to any malicious provocation and resolutely safeguard its territorial sovereignty and maritime rights and interests. Spokesperson Mao Ning made the remarks on Friday, reiterating that a Philippine coast guard vessel had entered waters near Ren'ai Jiao in China's Nansha Qundao without China's permission on Thursday morning. The measures taken by the China Coast Guard (CCG) in accordance with laws and regulations were justified and reasonable, Mao said. Following communication between the two sides, China promptly allowed the injured person to be transferred by a small boat on humanitarian grounds and provided necessary assistance, Mao added. Instead of showing appreciation, some individuals in the Philippines disregarded the facts, took information out of context and shifted blame onto China, Mao said. This again exposed their real intention of stirring up trouble and seeking attention, she said, calling such conduct disgraceful. Mao's remarks followed a statement issued on Thursday evening by CCG spokesperson Jiang Lue, who said Philippine coast guard vessel 4409 had traveled to waters near Ren'ai Jiao that day to evacuate an injured person from the Philippine warship illegally grounded there. Jiang also confirmed that out of humanitarian considerations, the Chinese side immediately allowed the Philippine side to transfer the injured person by small boat, and the CCG handled the matter in accordance with the law and regulations, and provided necessary assistance. Jiang said the Philippine side's remarks disregarded the facts, distorted the truth and sought to mislead the public. China has indisputable sovereignty over Nansha Qundao, including Ren'ai Jiao, and their adjacent waters, he said, warning the Philippine side to immediately stop its infringements, provocations and dissemination of false claims. Global Times

item.title: China rebuts US allegations of China-linked hacking activities, urges it to abandon double standards, political manipulation on cybersecurity: FM
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-09 15:54:00
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning China firmly opposes and combats hacking activities in accordance with law, while also firmly opposing the spread of false information and the creation of various kinds of noise for political purposes, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said on Friday. Mao made the remarks at a regular press conference in response to a question about US Justice Department officials claiming they are seizing seven internet domains allegedly linked to Chinese hackers accused of attempting to infiltrate critical infrastructure systems in the US and other countries. "Safeguarding cybersecurity is a common concern of both China and the US," Mao said. China urged the US to abandon double standards and political manipulation, engage with China through dialogue and consultation on an equal footing, jointly address cybersecurity risks, and work toward building peaceful, stable and mutually respectful China-US cyber relations. Global Times

item.title: Chinese, European teams confirm FAST discovery of first known evolving primordial pulsar triple
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-09 15:02:00
An artist's impression of the first known primordial pulsar triple system with a still-evolving companion star. Courtesy: Produced by Bureau of International Cooperation, Chinese Academy of Sciences China's FAST telescope has helped uncover the first known primordial pulsar triple with a still-evolving companion star, according to a statement sent to the Global Times by the National Astronomical Observatories (NAOC) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences. Chinese and European scientists independently confirmed the finding through shared data from observatories around the world. The system, known as PSR J0435+3233, consists of a pulsar, a white dwarf and a Sun-like star. Researchers believe the three were born together, making it a primordial system, but have since followed different paths as they aged. The Chinese study, led by Han Jinlin, a researcher at the NAOC, was published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters on Friday. A European team comprising scientists from Germany, the Netherlands, France and the UK independently analyzed similar archival data and reached the same conclusion about the system's triple nature. The parallel studies combined China's radio observations with data from international space missions and sky surveys. FAST, short for the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical radio Telescope and known as China's "Sky Eye," has discovered more than 1,000 pulsars since its completion, including a range of rare systems. PSR J0435+3233 was first detected on June 8, 2020, by an NAOC team conducting a drift-scan survey with FAST. The pulsar, a rapidly rotating neutron star, completes one rotation every 3.2 milliseconds. Researchers at the Xinjiang Astronomical Observatory then used FAST to monitor it for nearly five years, obtaining 192 timing measurements. They found that the pulsar and a white dwarf orbit their shared center of mass every eight days in an almost circular orbit. But the observations presented a puzzle: the pulsar appeared to be slowing down about 100 times faster than comparable millisecond pulsars. Those findings were published in Nature Astronomy in April. To investigate, Han's team combined FAST radio measurements with publicly available optical and infrared data from Gaia, 2MASS and Pan-STARRS, as well as long-term gamma-ray observations from the Fermi satellite. Together, these observations revealed a third companion: a star with roughly the mass of the Sun. The Chinese team calculated that this outer star takes about 73.5 years to circle the inner pair on an elongated orbit with an eccentricity of about 0.6. Its gravitational pull changes the inner pair's motion relative to Earth, altering the observed intervals between pulses and accounting for the unusually large apparent slowdown. Excluding systems with planetary companions, PSR J0435+3233 is only the second confirmed stellar triple containing a pulsar. The previously known system, PSR J0337+1715, was discovered using the US Green Bank Telescope and already consists of one pulsar and two white dwarfs. The presence of a star that has yet to become a stellar remnant gives astronomers a rare opportunity to study how such systems evolve. NAOC described the stellar triple as "extremely unique" because it contains a still-evolving star. In the researchers' proposed formation scenario, the most massive of the three stars began with about 20 times the Sun's mass and eventually exploded as a supernova, leaving behind the neutron star. Its closer companion, initially several times as massive as the Sun, later became a white dwarf. The least massive star, farther from the inner pair, is still undergoing stellar evolution. Over time, the outer star is also expected to become a white dwarf, leaving a pulsar with two white-dwarf companions, according to NAOC. NAOC described the discovery as a milestone made possible by research teams in China and abroad building on one another's work and combining observations across multiple wavelengths. It demonstrated the value of open data sharing and collaborative efforts to tackle scientific challenges, the observatory said. The clear and pronounced gravitational interactions among the three members make this evolving primordial system a valuable natural laboratory for testing fundamental theories of gravity, including the strong equivalence principle, the NAOC said. The system also offers a rare opportunity to study the complex evolution of triple-star systems and explore astrophysical processes in extreme environments.

item.title: Indonesian president launches 11 Chinese-backed downstream projects
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-09 13:45:00
Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto (4th L) attends the launch ceremony for 11 Chinese-backed downstream projects at the Weda Bay Industrial Park in Central Halmahera, North Maluku, Indonesia, Oct. 8, 2026. (Xinhua/Cheng Yiheng) Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto on Thursday launched 11 Chinese-backed downstream projects worth an estimated 10.2 billion U.S. dollars at the Weda Bay Industrial Park in Central Halmahera, North Maluku. Prabowo also witnessed the park's first export of electric vehicle (EV) batteries produced by Chinese enterprises. He said the export marked "a notable milestone" in the government's downstreaming policy to increase the added value of natural resources and strengthen the EV industry. "This is concrete proof that our downstreaming policy is on the right track, and we will continue to advance it to the fullest extent possible," Prabowo said. According to Prabowo, cumulative investment in the park has surpassed 20 billion dollars, with an additional 7 billion dollars planned for future expansion. The industrial zone has created more than 100,000 jobs since its development began. This photo taken on Oct. 8, 2026 shows a partial view of the Weda Bay Industrial Park in Central Halmahera, North Maluku, Indonesia. (Xinhua/Cheng Yiheng)

item.title: Chinese envoy condemns Japan's remilitarization push at UN, warns of threat to peace
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-09 12:56:00
Sun Xiaobo, director-general of the Chinese Foreign Ministry's Department of Arms Control, speaks during the general debate of the First Committee of the 81st UN General Assembly on October 8, 2026, as head of the Chinese delegation. The committee deals with disarmament and international security. Photo: Screenshot of CCTV News A Chinese envoy on Thursday condemned Japan's accelerating remilitarization at the United Nations, warning that it had become a major threat to regional peace and stability and urging Tokyo to fulfill its nuclear non-proliferation obligations. Sun Xiaobo, director-general of the Chinese Foreign Ministry's Department of Arms Control, addressed the general debate of the First Committee of the 81st UN General Assembly as head of the Chinese delegation. The committee deals with disarmament and international security. Sun said the postwar international order, the UN-centered international system and the basic norms governing international relations based on the purposes and principles of the UN Charter were facing serious challenges, according to CCTV News. Noting that this year marks the 81st anniversary of the UN's founding and the 80th anniversary of the opening of the Tokyo Trials, Sun stressed the need to learn from history and resist attempts to turn back the clock. Japan joined the UN on the condition that it acknowledged the crimes of militarism and accepted the UN Charter in its entirety, Sun said. Yet its current administration denies Japan's history of aggression, glorifies war crimes and pays homage to World War II war criminals while expanding its military capabilities and accelerating re-militarization, Sun said. Sun also denounced calls by senior Japanese officials for unrestricted debate on acquiring nuclear weapons, saying they reflected attempts to abandon the country's Three Non-Nuclear Principles. He said such moves were a serious provocation against and violation of the international nuclear non-proliferation regime. The principles commit Japan to neither possess or produce nuclear weapons, nor permitting their introduction into the country, according to Japan's Foreign Ministry. Sun's remarks followed comments by Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi on a BS Fuji program on September 28. Discussing the possession of nuclear weapons and nuclear-powered submarines, Koizumi called for debate "without taboos or predetermined conclusions," Kyodo News reported. He claimed that refusing to allow even a discussion was at odds with his sense of urgency over security threats. Sun also criticized Japan's proposal to remove the "enemy state" clauses from the UN Charter, calling it the latest example of Tokyo challenging the postwar international order under the guise of becoming a "normal country." Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi called for the clauses to be removed during her address to the UN General Assembly in New York on September 22, Kyodo News reported. Sun urged Japan to reflect deeply on its history of aggression, make a clean break with militarism, abandon its re-militarization plans and fulfill its obligations under international law on nuclear non-proliferation, according to CCTV News. Global Times

item.title: Crime drama leads China's National Day box office as market dips from last year
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-09 12:17:00
Spectators look at posters at a cinema in Hai'an City, east China's Jiangsu Province, Oct. 6, 2026. (Photo by Xu Jingbo/Xinhua) Crime drama "Traces of Justice" topped China's National Day holiday box office, in a market that fell from a year earlier, with some analysts citing the absence of a blockbuster-scale title. The seven-day holiday frame ending on Wednesday generated 1.165 billion yuan (about 173 million U.S. dollars) from nearly 32 million admissions, according to the China Film Administration. Daily takings exceeded 100 million yuan throughout, but the total was well below last year's eight-day holiday, which grossed 1.835 billion yuan, according to ticketing platform Maoyan. "Traces of Justice" grossed 423 million yuan. It was followed on the charts by comedy "Mr. & Mrs. Pardon," imported horror title "Resident Evil," war drama "Once Upon a Time in the Middle East" and animated feature "Peppa Pig: Perfect Holiday." The top three earners accounted for more than 70 percent of total revenue. Directed and co-written by Chen Sicheng, "Traces of Justice" is based on the life and work of renowned trace-evidence expert Cui Daozhi. The film, starring Zhang Yi, follows investigators as they solve challenging cases using forensic evidence like fingerprints and bite marks, while also tracing the development of forensic techniques in China over several decades. A report released Thursday by the Maoyan Research Institute found that the share of multi-person movie outings during the National Day holiday fell to its lowest level in six years, while solo moviegoers made up 25.7 percent of admissions, also a six-year high. The report said family demand was not fully met, and that the continued strength of some summer holdovers reflected a lack of new family-oriented releases. "This year's top three films each found their own path to success, but audience interest remained relatively subdued overall because there was no blockbuster-scale title capable of generating broader excitement," said Lai Li, a Maoyan analyst. Lai added that as audiences become more selective, there will be a greater need for innovation in both content and form. Among the standouts was "Resident Evil," which opened on Oct. 5. Lai said the globally recognized franchise and better-than-expected word of mouth converted core fans into ticket buyers and helped boost its box office and buzz. Other indicators were more resilient. Maoyan counted 12,800 cinemas and 79,400 screens in operation, both the highest for a National Day holiday in six years. After a soft opening day, the market held up well, with new releases lifting daily takings on the third and fifth days. Fifth-day revenue rose 22.9 percent from the previous day to become the holiday's strongest single day, which Maoyan said underscored the role of new film supply in stimulating the market. Chen Jin, an analyst at film data platform Beacon, expects leading titles to continue supporting the box office through mid-to-late October. Maoyan forecasts Chinese mainland box office totals of 670 million yuan for "Traces of Justice," 550 million yuan for "Resident Evil" and 390 million yuan for "Mr. & Mrs. Pardon." The Chinese mainland's annual box office has surpassed 30.7 billion yuan so far this year.

item.title: Tsai Ing-wen's provocative trip to the US: an outright sellout of Taiwan: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-09 00:00:00
Tsai Ing-wen Photo:VCG The essence of Tsai Ing-wen's provocative trip to the US is to sacrifice Taiwan's industrial development in a bid to curry political favor with Washington. It amounts to gambling with the lives and livelihoods of Taiwan residents and using the island's valuable resources to secure verbal endorsements from certain US politicians in exchange for the DPP's own political survival. Tsai Ing-wen, former leader of the Taiwan region, is on a provocative trip to the US. Upon her arrival, she first met with former US House speaker Nancy Pelosi. The two washed-up politicians, who have long exploited the "Taiwan independence" agenda for political gains, once again colluded to recycle the same old rhetoric and remind the world of their fading political relevance. Tsai then delivered a speech at Stanford University's annual DEFCON Technology & National Security Conference, where she touted Taiwan's position in the semiconductor sector and global artificial intelligence (AI) supply chains. She hyped up the island's so-called "democratic resilience" and its "position at the center of the first island chain," smeared the Chinese mainland's policy toward Taiwan, and deliberately framed the Taiwan question as an "international security issue." Taken as a whole, Tsai's US trip is nothing less than an act of selling out Taiwan: It sacrifices the interests of the Taiwan residents in pursuit of the separatist "Taiwan independence" agenda, while offering nothing to safeguard the well-being of the people on the island. It is well known that Taiwan's semiconductor industry is the product of decades of hard work and investment by industrialists on the island. In recent years, it has become an important engine of the island's economic development and a critical link in global supply chains. Against the backdrop of the rapid development of AI technology in the Chinese mainland, this sector should have become an opportunity for cross-Straits integrated development and mutually beneficial cooperation, rather than a political bargaining chip for "Taiwan independence" separatist forces to pursue personal gains and collude with external powers. Yet in the eyes of Tsai and the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) authorities, the island's hard-won industrial advantages are little more than tools for political maneuvering. During her provocative trip to the US, Tsai has actively tied Taiwan's cutting-edge technology industries to Washington's geopolitical maneuvering, catered to the US strategy of "using Taiwan to contain China," and deliberately securitized and politicized economic and industrial interests. It is worth noting that Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. (TSMC) has already brought its advanced technology to Arizona and begun mass production there, strengthening the US domestic supply of advanced chips. The essence of Tsai's speech at Stanford University is to sacrifice Taiwan's industrial development in a bid to curry political favor with Washington. It is an act of flattery and an outright sellout of Taiwan. Tsai currently serves as the campaign headquarters chairperson for several DPP candidates running for "city mayors" and "county chiefs," and Taiwan media generally believe that she hopes to use her trip to the US to raise her personal profile and boost the prospects in local elections. Such an approach - trading industrial interests for political gains and sacrificing the public interest for personal ambitions - seriously undermines the foundation of Taiwan's development and harms the long-term interests of all residents in Taiwan. Moreover, during her visit to the US, Tsai made a great deal of hype about Taiwan's so-called "difficult-to-replace role," deliberately stoking cross-Straits confrontation and exaggerating tensions in the Taiwan Straits in an attempt to expand the space for "Taiwan independence" separatist activities by binding the Taiwan region more closely to the US. Such an approach won't bring Taiwan genuine "security." Instead, it will only heighten the risks of a crisis in the Taiwan Straits. A private trip by a former politician can't change the fact that the US regards Taiwan as a pawn, or even a disposable pawn, in its "Indo-Pacific Strategy." Nor can it change the genuine feelings and rational judgment of voters on the island. According to the latest poll conducted by Taiwan's media outlet My Formosa, as many as 60.3 percent of respondents expressed a lack of confidence that Washington would safeguard Taiwan's interests, including 30.2 percent who said they had "no confidence at all." Various signs suggest that the deception of "seeking independence by relying on the US" has long lost its effectiveness on the island. Similar polls have been released by multiple organizations, including institutions on the island that lean toward either the blue or green political camps, as well as US think tanks and media outlets. Despite their different backgrounds, the findings of these polls point to the same conclusion: Mainstream public opinion in Taiwan does not believe that the US will come to Taiwan's defense. Public opinion cannot be defied, nor can the trust of the people be squandered. For years, the DPP authorities have engaged in self-deception by beautifying US-Taiwan relations and touting support from external forces. At the same time, they have misled the Taiwan public to gain votes, continuously sought to externalize and internationalize the Taiwan question, and recklessly provoked cross-Straits confrontation. The essence of Tsai's visit to the US is to gamble with the lives and livelihoods of Taiwan residents, using the island's valuable resources to secure verbal endorsements from certain US politicians in exchange for the DPP's own political survival. What appears to be a high-profile political spectacle is, in reality, an exercise in isolation and a loss of public support. Ultimately, it is nothing more than a futile political performance. Taiwan is a part of China, and its future and destiny will always rest in the hands of all Chinese people. No matter how Tsai and others like her collude with external forces or hype up the "Taiwan independence" agenda, they cannot change the established fact that Taiwan is part of China, nor can they stop the historical trend toward national reunification. If "Taiwan independence" separatist forces refuse to abandon their illusion of "seeking independence by relying on external forces" and insist on using the island's industrial capabilities to curry political favor while treating the lives and livelihoods of the people as bargaining chips, they will ultimately only harm and ruin Taiwan, bring about their own destruction, and see their names written on the wall of shame.

item.title: GT Voice: 'Overcapacity' must not become a new pretext for trade protectionism
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-08 22:01:00
China trade economy File photo: VCG On the sidelines of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development Trade Committee meeting, trade ministers from a dozen economies signed on to a US-led statement calling for actions to address structural excess capacity and production, the Office of the US Trade Representative said on Wednesday. While the joint statement does not name any specific country, it nonetheless signals a rising tide of trade protectionism that deserves high vigilance from the international community. Specifically, the statement identified sectors of concern as including but not limited to: autos and electric vehicles (EVs), batteries, chemicals, foundational semiconductors, and solar panels. The list itself is telling: It targets precisely the core sectors driving the ongoing global energy transition and technological upgrading. By singling out these industries as areas of "overcapacity" concern, the statement makes clear that its real purpose is not to resolve any genuine market imbalance but to provide a pretext for policies aimed at restricting specific industries. The rise of these industries stems from breakthrough advances in the relevant technologies. Technological breakthroughs tend to give rise to new industries, which in turn generate strong market demand for emerging products - most directly reflected in the sustained surge and continuous expansion of global demand for green and intelligent products. Take the photovoltaic (PV) industry as an example. According to a report by the International Energy Agency in 2025, the amount of installed renewable power is predicted to more than double by 2030, and solar PV will account for about 80 percent of the global increase in renewable power capacity. Clearly, the global green industry is far from saturated - so how could it possibly be suffering from "overcapacity"? Likewise, the penetration of EVs remains in the single digits across most regions worldwide. Demand for energy storage batteries continues to surge alongside the rapid expansion of renewable energy deployment, and structural supply gaps persist across multiple downstream semiconductor sectors. To judge the capacity of these industries from such a narrow perspective is to ignore entirely the broader trend of growing global demand. In recent decades, the global division of labor has deepened along the lines of comparative advantage. Drawing on their respective resource endowments, technological accumulation and market needs, different economies have gradually formed industrial layouts with different emphases. The large-scale concentrated production of certain industries in specific regions is itself a product of natural market competition. The cost reductions, efficiency gains and technological iteration delivered by economies of scale have ultimately benefited consumers in virtually every market through global trade networks. Yet some economies now disregard this basic fact entirely, judging the situation solely by short-term supply-demand conditions in localized markets and by competitive pressure on domestic industries - arbitrarily slapping the "overcapacity" label on other countries' advantageous industries. Such a standard is fundamentally untenable and runs counter to the long-standing core logic of the free trade system. More worrying still, "overcapacity" is gradually becoming a new pretext for trade protectionism in some economies. In recent years, the global economic recovery has been fraught with twists and turns, as geopolitical conflicts, inflationary volatility and shrinking demand compound one another. Faced with declining industrial competitiveness and prominent structural difficulties at home, some economies are unwilling to address their own problems through deeper reform, industrial upgrading and technological innovation. Instead, they externalize domestic economic pressures by redefining normal outcomes of market competition as structural problems that require policy intervention. The danger of such conceptual manipulation is profound: Once "overcapacity" becomes a policy tool that can be arbitrarily defined, any industry with enjoying advantages in cost, technology or scale can be targeted at will. Such a trend could systematically undermine the rules-based foundation of global trade. This approach - using capacity governance as a pretext for trade protection — may appear to safeguard domestic industrial interests, but it will ultimately backfire on the global economy and severely damage the stability and resilience of global industrial and supply chains. The World Economic Forum has said that fragmentation is already costing the global economy $213 billion to $307 billion annually, while adding 0.2 to 0.3 percentage points to global inflation. Ultimately, consumers worldwide would face higher prices and fewer choices, while industries that could otherwise achieve large-scale, efficient production would be less motivated to keep investing in research and upgrading, as their market space is artificially compressed. In this sense, labeling competitive industries as examples of "overcapacity" may sound sophisticated, but it essentially erodes the foundation for long-term global economic growth. Such a path leads nowhere and should never be taken.

item.title: Respect is earned, not demanded – Japan's fuss over a diplomatic title rings hollow
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-08 20:25:00
Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi raises her hand to answer a question during a session of the House of Councillors Budget Committee at the National Diet in Tokyo, Japan on November 12, 2025. Photo: VCG In a news briefing on Wednesday, Japanese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Toshihiro Kitamura said that Tokyo had relayed its concerns to Beijing after the Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun referred to the Japanese prime minister only as "Sanae Takaichi" at a recent press conference. Showing "appropriate respect to the leader of another country" is a matter of "international protocol," said Kitamura. The news provoked irony. The international community sees clearly: The one that has truly wantonly trampled on international etiquette, undermined basic diplomatic principles, and challenged the post-war international order has always been certain Japanese politicians. After all, diplomatic etiquette goes far beyond mere titles and addresses. For some time now, the Japanese right-wing forces, led by Sanae Takaichi, have been constantly crossing diplomatic red lines and trampling on the boundaries of international relations, with a series of provocations against China. When the Takaichi cabinet repeatedly tests the waters on historical accountability, remains obstinate on the Taiwan question, refuses to retract erroneous remarks, and accelerates constitutional revision and military expansion - breaking free from the constraints of its pacifist constitution - they are violating international ethics, diplomatic etiquette, and the post-war order. While Japan recklessly harms the interests of other countries and crosses the bottom line of international relations, it nitpicks at minor details of diplomatic titles, demanding that other countries grant it so-called "appropriate respect." Doesn't this sophisticated self-serving double standard completely deviate from the essence of international etiquette? A look at the trajectory of the Chinese Foreign Ministry's recent rhetoric over Tokyo reveals a clear logic: from "Japanese prime minister" to "the incumbent leader of Japan," and finally to addressing her simply by name. This shift underscores a simple truth: Respect has always been mutual; the bottom line must not be crossed, and restraint does not equal indulgence. Since Tokyo often tries to conflate Takaichi and her cabinet with the entirety of Japan to muddy the waters, Chinese observers have noted that Beijing's wording achieves a precise political distinction - separating the reckless agenda of Sanae Takaichi and her likes from the rational elements of the Japanese nation and its people. It signals that China's stern warning is directed not at the Japanese public, but strictly at the radical Japanese right-wing politicians led by Takaichi. On the other hand, Beijing has not slammed the door shut and continues to engage with Japanese friendly figures, economic groups, and rational voices from civil society, striving to steer bilateral relations back onto the right track. Instead of obsessing over a title, Japanese politicians need to reflect on how to act as a good neighbor to regional countries, including China. As an ancient Chinese saying goes, "He who tied the bell on the tiger must untie it." Rather than nursing a fragile ego over whether a spokesperson uttered the word "prime minister," Tokyo should put its energy where it matters - rectifying its damaging actions against China-Japan relations and figuring out what it actually takes to build a "constructive and stable relationship" with China. At the end of the day, respect is earned, not demanded.
